verdicts.quote: the top part of an animal's body, between its neck and its tail
verdicts.reason: An animal's back is its upper surface, not necessarily a body part bounded between the neck and tail; the wording excludes much of the back in common use.
The expression is common in both American and British English, so an American-only regional label is misleading.

reviewers.summary: The entry is largely accurate and learner-appropriate. Correct the animal-back definition and remove the misleading American-only label from “have someone's back.”

verdicts.reason: Items such as 'back door', 'back seat', and 'back room' use 'back' as an adjective or noun adjunct and are better categorized as compound nouns or cross-referenced under back-adj.
'back to back' functions adverbially or adjectivally rather than as an idiomatic noun phrase, though it is commonly filed under the noun headword.

reviewers.summary: The entry is exceptionally well crafted and adheres closely to lexicographical house standards. Only minor classification notes arise regarding noun adjunct collocations in sense 2 and the placement of the adverbial phrase 'back to back'.
